messages.body_plain:
Hi Arthur and Bernd,

Thank you for the incredibly fast response!

I can confirm that the following works to calculate diversity metrics for individuals within a population. Very nice hack :)

gl <- gl.reassign.pop(testset.gl <http://testset.gl>,as.pop="id")

popNames(gl)

out <- gl.report.heterozygosity(gl)

Both of you mentioned the incorporation of standardizing sampling size of either 1) population or 2) loci as being on the "to-do list." Some thoughts below to hopefully make it easier for you?

1) Bashalkhanov's model: this paper developed and validated (with natural population data) a metric for this: “A simple method for estimating genetic diversity in large populations from finite sample sizes: Bashalkhanov et al. BMC Genetics 2009, 10:84doi:10.1186/1471-2156-10-84.

Perhaps this model could be incorporated, loops through all the SNPs, and applies a correction at the end for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni)?

2) Could borrow from the microbial literature that routinely calculates diversity metrics across samples of varying read abundance. Rarefaction used to be the norm but now negative binomial and zero-inflated Gaussian mixture models (package metagenomeSeq) are now being used within the wonderful Phyloseq package.

Waste Not, Want Not: Why Rarefying Microbiome Data Is Inadmissible, McMurdie and Holmes https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003531

3) The following are quick and dirty but not ideal:

H0/nLoc

H0/nInd per population

Anyways, thank you for the help 😊

Cheers,

Kate

Re: command gl2fasta
messages.body_plain:
Hi Emmanuel,

Not sure what the issue is there. You have 580 loci ranging from 20 to 69 bp if your data was produced by DArT (use gl.report.taglength to see distribution -- see attached report for the testset.gl <http://testset.gl>), so you would expect approximately 580x69 bases in each record in your fastA file. That comes to 40020.

You have only 30,380 presumably because not all sequence tags in your dataset were 69 bp long, and because the script takes out sequence tags that have been over-trimmed in removing the adaptors (taking the SNP position with the adaptor -- happens infrequently when the adaptor sequence and the terminal end of the sequence tag are fairly similar by chance).

To check this out, you could remove all loci for which the sequence tag is less than 69

gl2 <- gl.filter.taglength(tr4.o,lower=69)

then

gl2fasta(gl2,outfile="tr4.outgroups_SNPs.fas",method=2,outpath="~PROJETS/beta1")

And you should have around 30,380, the remaining distortion owing to the removal of the few sequence tags where the SNP was removed when the tag was trimmed of adaptors.

Can you give this a try?

A

messages.body_plain:
Hi Farhad,

In that case, by far the best option is to list your first service when submitting samples to DArT for a second service so that they can run both data sets through their pipelines together. This is the best option because calling the SNPs is not a locus by locus exercise, but the DArT folk examine the data manually and make decisions on thresholds based on global attributes. As an extreme case, some loci that would not make the mark when examining the first dataset may do so in the combined analysis.

You can ask DArT to combine your two services into one analysis, and maybe they will do it for no or a minimal charge?

A
